profiles.name: Guy Chichester
profiles.description: Guy Chichester was a Navy veteran who moved from Long Island to Rye, NH, and a co-founder of the Clamshell Alliance in 1976 and a perennial figure in New England anti-nuclear and environmental organizing. Later served as president of the Seacoast Anti-Pollution League. In a celebrated act of civil disobedience he sawed down a Seabrook Station emergency-warning siren pole, was charged with criminal mischief (a Class B felony), and was acquitted by jury.
profiles.finding: Legacy/Seacoastonline obituary identifies Clamshell founder and siren-pole action; obituary portrait and family gallery remain leads needing original resolution/credit inspection.

profiles.name: Sukie Rice
profiles.description: Sukie Rice was an AFSC staffer in Boston who, with Elizabeth Boardman, designed and led the nonviolence training that made the April 30, 1977 Seabrook occupation famously disciplined. Joined the Durham (Maine) Monthly Meeting of Friends in 1979, raised a family in Freeport, and spent her last two decades supporting vulnerable children in western Kenya through Friends of Kakamega.
profiles.finding: Deployed captioned 1976 Green Mountain Post Films portrait via Narco News. Rejected 2013 Laura Garcia landscape for tiny face. AFSC obituary gives July17 2020 age74, conflicting with existing August15 2020 age75; unrelated fields preserved and flagged for separate correction.

profiles.name: Greg Franklin
profiles.description: Greg Franklin was identified by The Black Panther as a Black Panther Party member whom Los Angeles police beat and arrested with Robert “Sharief” Kendrick in April 1977. Police accused Franklin of assault and battery on a peace officer. The available contemporary report describes the charge as false, but a booking record, release date and final disposition have not been located.
profiles.finding: Exact-name Panther/1977 searches yielded no independently verified portrait; contemporary Panther April1977 report remains archive lead.

profiles.name: Raisa Nemikin
profiles.description: Staff member of the Episcopal Church's National Commission on Hispanic Affairs jailed in 1977 alongside Maria Cueto for refusing to testify before a federal grand jury investigating the FALN. profiles.name: Ben Lenard
profiles.description: Ben Lenard was a Black worker at International Harvester in Chicago who, driving home from work on January 31, 1977, was struck by another car. When police finally arrived, the other driver — a white woman with no license or insurance — claimed Lenard had assaulted her; without any investigation the officers handcuffed him, beat him nearly beyond recognition in the squad car, beat him again at the jail, stripped him, threw him into a cell, opened the windows in zero-degree weather and doused him with cold water. His family was able to bail him out only after being told he was being "processed," and took him to a hospital. Reconstructed from Revolutionary Cause (August Twenty-Ninth Movement M-L), March 1977, which reported the case as part of the pattern of racist police frame-ups; the disposition of the charge against him has not been located.
profiles.finding: Revolutionary Cause March1977 and November1977 match Chicago case; DePaul/Argonne computing faculty namesake not linked, rejected.

profiles.name: Curtis Jones Jr.
profiles.description:
Corporal Curtis Jones Jr. was one of the "Camp Pendleton 14," a group of Black Marines court-martialed after they confronted an active-duty Ku Klux Klan presence at Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton on November 13, 1976 — raiding a barracks they believed was hosting a Klan meeting amid a wave of on-base cross-burnings and Klan literature. The Black Panther reported that Jones, charged with one count of conspiracy and six counts of aggravated assault, was the first of about ten Black Marines ordered before a court-martial board and was held in the brig in solitary for over eight months, while the white Klansmen were quietly transferred and never punished.

Black Marine corporal, one of the 'Camp Pendleton 14' court-martialed after defending themselves against Ku Klux Klan attacks at Camp Pendleton in 1976; sentenced to three months at hard labor, demoted and fined. The Black Panther Vol. 17 no.3 (1977).

profiles.name: Edward Gullion
profiles.description: Edward Patrick Gullion Jr. was a member of the Fred Hampton Unit of the People's Forces, the clandestine leftist cell behind the August 7, 1976 bombings of a National Guard armory in Dorchester, an Eastern Airlines plane at Logan Airport, the Essex County Courthouse in Newburyport, and a post office in Seabrook, New Hampshire. Placed on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list (#344) in August 1976, he was arrested on October 22, 1976 in Providence, Rhode Island, where he was working at a jewelry store, and was convicted of federal explosives charges. Little is documented about his life after release.

profiles.name: Lureida Torres
profiles.description:
Lureida Torres was a twenty-six-year-old New York City schoolteacher and a member of the Puerto Rican Socialist Party (PSP), on the staff of the party's newspaper Claridad, when she was jailed in 1976 for refusing to cooperate with a federal grand jury. Imprisoned in New York on June 26, 1976 for civil contempt, Torres had declined to testify before a grand jury that was ostensibly investigating bombings by the Armed Forces of National Liberation (FALN) — an inquiry the PSP and independence leader Juan Mari Bras denounced as a "fishing expedition" and "witch-hunt" against the Puerto Rican independence movement, noting that neither Torres nor the party had any connection to the FALN.

A federal judge rejected the argument that her continued jailing was purely punitive, and a national "Campaign to Free Lureida Torres" organized demonstrations and a petition drive directed at U.S. Attorney General Edward Levi. Torres, who said she would never testify, was released on October 28, 1976 after completing a four-month sentence.
profiles.finding: Militant1976 issue4027 caption identifies Lureida at center being escorted; crop/quality/rights inspection pending. AAAS photographer credit is not proof of a portrait of her.

profiles.name: Filipina Narciso
profiles.description:
Filipina Narciso was one of two Filipina immigrant nurses at the Veterans Administration Medical Center in Ann Arbor, Michigan — with co-defendant Leonora Perez — prosecuted in a case widely condemned as a racist frame-up.

Over several months in 1975, an unusual cluster of patients at the hospital suffered sudden respiratory failure — attributed to the unauthorized injection of the paralytic drug Pavulon into their IV lines, with ten deaths. After an FBI investigation, the two nurses, both recent immigrants, were charged in 1976; the patients who had identified them died before trial.

At a 1977 trial in U.S. District Court, the nurses were acquitted of murder but found guilty of poisoning and conspiracy to poison. The trial was marred by overt anti-Filipino racism — a prosecution witness called them "slant-eyed bitches," and the government floated the notion of a "nationwide conspiracy of Filipino nurses to murder veterans." Trial judge Philip Pratt set the guilty verdicts aside, finding the jury had been swayed by the prosecution's prejudicial conduct, and the government dropped all charges in 1978 after a new U.S. attorney concluded the public did not support the prosecution. No other suspect was ever charged, and the case became a landmark rallying point for Filipino-American and immigrant communities.
profiles.finding: Ann Arbor District Library Larry E Wright1976 images and Commons1977 press image located. Need inspect individual positioning, original rights and clean crop.

profiles.name: Mark Cook
profiles.description:
Mark Cook was the only African-American member of the George Jackson Brigade and the last to join the Pacific Northwest militant prisoner-solidarity formation. He participated in the January 23, 1976 Tukwila bank robbery that killed Brigade member Bruce Seidel and led to the arrest of Ed Mead and John Sherman; he avoided arrest at the scene. Days later, he carried out the armed liberation of John Sherman from Harborview Medical Center in Seattle, where Sherman was being held under guard for medical treatment of her bank-robbery wounds; a King County deputy was wounded in the operation. Cook was arrested shortly afterward and convicted in Washington state court. He served 24 years in the Washington State Penitentiary at Walla Walla — the longest of any of the Brigade’s members.

Inside, he organized a chapter of the Black Panther Party at Walla Walla, founded the PIVOT post-release re-entry program, and organized the long-running CONvention prison-organizing seminar. He was released in 2000.
profiles.finding: Final Straw/Burning Books lecture and University of Washington Seattle Panther project are strong leads; British sexologist namesake rejected. Portrait not yet extracted.

profiles.name: José Jacques Medina
profiles.description: José Jacques Medina was a Mexican political exile, attorney and labor organizer in Los Angeles and a leader of CASA (Centro de Acción Social Autónomo), which organized undocumented workers. A veteran of Mexico's 1968 student-worker movement who had defended its political prisoners, he fled Mexico and was arrested by federal agents in March 1976 and turned over to the INS on an "illegal entry" charge. The Black Panther reported his fight against deportation and his denied bid for political asylum, framing it as U.S. collaboration with Mexican repression. He was later a Mexican federal deputy.
profiles.finding: Una Citta2015 interview identifies Mexican1968 activist/US immigrant organizer, official deputy records corroborate; portrait and credit inspection pending.

profiles.name: Bruce Seidel
profiles.description: Bruce Seidel was a former University of Illinois economics graduate student turned prison-rights activist who helped found the Seattle-based George Jackson Brigade. Shot and killed January 23, 1976 by police during the GJB's failed bank robbery in Tukwila, Washington. Killed before trial.
profiles.finding: Search returned GJB context but unrelated television producer Bruce Seidel; producer rejected, no verified portrait.

profiles.name: Ed Mead
profiles.description:
Ed Mead was the principal theorist of the George Jackson Brigade, a Seattle-based militant prison-solidarity formation that conducted a series of bombings of state and corporate targets and bank expropriations in the Pacific Northwest from 1975 to 1978. He was arrested on January 23, 1976, after an attempted bank robbery at the Pacific National Bank in Tukwila, Washington in which Brigade member Bruce Seidel was killed and Mead was wounded. He was convicted of attempted bank robbery and conspiracy and sentenced to 30 years at the Walla Walla State Penitentiary in Washington.

Inside, he founded Men Against Sexism, the prisoners’ gay-and-anti-rape organization that confronted the white-supremacist gang structures running 1970s Walla Walla, and edited Prison Legal News for many years. He was released in 1993 after 17 years and has continued to be a major figure in U.S. anarchist and prison-abolition writing.

Founding member of the George Jackson Brigade, a Pacific Northwest revolutionary cell active 1975-1978. Captured January 23, 1976 during the failed Tukwila (WA) Pacific National Bank robbery in which fellow brigadier Bruce Seidel was killed and John Sherman was wounded. Held at Washington State Penitentiary at Walla Walla, where he co-founded Men Against Sexism. Released in 1993 after 18 years for his political actions (35 years of his life were spent in prisons total). Continued radical organizing post-release.
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives1992 tribunal program explicitly includes Ed Mead portrait before bookshelves; Kersplebedeb2023 obituary/El Salto WallaWalla image also leads. Geologist/politician namesakes rejected.

profiles.name: John Sherman
profiles.description: John Sherman met Ed Mead at McNeil Island federal prison in the late 1960s and later joined the George Jackson Brigade. He was wounded and captured during the January 23, 1976 Tukwila bank robbery, freed from custody by Mark Cook on March 10, 1976, and recaptured with Therese Coupez and Janine Bertram on March 21, 1978. Sherman was convicted in federal court in July 1978, escaped from USP Lompoc in March 1979, was recaptured in Golden, Colorado, on December 17, 1981, and was released on parole in 1998. He later became a spiritual teacher.
profiles.finding: Search dominated nineteenth-century senator and modern intelligence official; both rejected. GJB/spiritual-teacher continuity and portrait unresolved.

profiles.name: Juan Haro
profiles.description: Juan Haro was a leader and head of security for the Denver Chicano movement organization Crusade for Justice. Federal prosecutors accused him of possessing four unregistered hand grenades after police informant José Cordova Jr. claimed Haro supplied them. A jury convicted Haro on January 22, 1976, and he received four concurrent six-year terms. In the separate state prosecution alleging a plot to bomb Denver police stations, a jury acquitted him in 1977 after the defense exposed serious problems with Cordova’s testimony and the government’s evidence. Haro served 22 months of the federal sentence and later wrote about the case in his memoir, The Ultimate Betrayal.

profiles.name: Steven Soliah
profiles.description: House painter and brother of Kathleen Soliah, a member of the SLA's second formation and a roommate of Michael Bortin. Captured with the Harrises, Patty Hearst and Wendy Yoshimura on September 18, 1975 and indicted in 1976 for the Carmichael bank robbery and the Opsahl killing. Acquitted at his federal bank-robbery trial in 1976 after an alibi witness testified he was with her in San Francisco at the time. Never re-charged with the Opsahl killing in 2002 because of double-jeopardy from the federal acquittal.

profiles.name: Richard Thomas
profiles.description: Richard Thomas was a member of Philadelphia’s Black Unity Council and one of six men whom prosecutors identified with a group called “The Revolutionaries” in the 1970 Cobbs Creek case. He went underground after being accused of taking part in a plan that prosecutors said led to the killing of Fairmount Park Police Sergeant Frank Von Colln and the wounding of Officer Joseph Harrington. Thomas remained underground for twenty-six years before his arrest in suburban Chicago in March 1996. At trial, Thomas maintained that he had fled because he feared being railroaded or shot by police. Unlike the five codefendants who received life sentences, he was acquitted by a Philadelphia jury on November 3, 1999. The prosecution and acquittal occurred against the backdrop of Frank Rizzo’s crackdown on Black political organizations and federal COINTELPRO repression.
profiles.finding: Poison Tree history corroborates Philadelphia case and acquittal; no verified portrait. Actor namesake must not be used.

profiles.name: John Lynch
profiles.description: John Lynch was a Florida-born defendant in the federal prosecution known as the Tucson Six. Prosecutors accused six men of a conspiracy to obtain weapons for the Irish Republican Army. A contemporary Tucson account describes local supporters visiting all six defendants as prisoners at the federal correctional institution and helping secure bail for members of the group. Lynch denied knowing the four Irish-born defendants. After a two-month trial, all six were acquitted in April 1994.

profiles.name: James Dixon
profiles.description: James Dixon was jailed in Chicago after an August 2, 1975 incident in which a police sergeant was wounded. He pleaded guilty to aggravated battery in July 1976 under a time-served agreement. Investigators subsequently established that the sergeant had accidentally shot himself with an illegal pen gun. Dixon’s conviction was vacated and the charge dismissed on August 20, 1976. The exact physical release date remains unresolved.

profiles.name: Bruce Andrew Baechler

profiles.name: Dessie Woods
profiles.description: Black woman from Georgia who in 1975 shot and killed a white insurance agent who attempted to rape her and her companion Cheryl Todd. Sentenced to 22 years in prison and became the focus of a major national defense campaign through the late 1970s, including by PFOC. Released in 1981. Documented in PFOC Breakthrough magazine.

profiles.name: Roy Lee Patterson
profiles.description: Roy Lee Patterson was a decorated Black Marine sergeant arrested after the May 4, 1975 deaths of a Georgia state trooper and a Cordele police officer during a struggle over the trooper’s gun. Patterson said he acted in defense of himself and his family after the trooper attacked him. A majority-white jury convicted him in September 1975 and imposed two consecutive life sentences. The Eleventh Circuit overturned the convictions in 1984 because of an unconstitutional jury instruction. A 1986 retrial ended with nine jurors voting to acquit and three voting to convict, producing a mistrial; he remained imprisoned while another trial was prepared in 1987. His eventual release date remains unresolved.
profiles.finding: Georgia case records match; Roy Neal obituary and Texas cemetery namesakes not verified, rejected. No usable portrait.

profiles.name: Leonard Alexander
profiles.description: Leonard Alexander was a Black inmate at the Correctional Training Facility at Soledad who, in a letter published by The Black Panther in 1980, appealed to the Prisoners' Rights Task Force for help defending himself and twelve other Black prisoners being tried on murder, assault and conspiracy charges arising from racial disturbances at Soledad in 1979. He alleged the district attorney and the Department of Corrections used perjured informant testimony, rewarded prosecution witnesses with sentence commutations, and forced Black defendants before all-white juries. The charges stemmed from the December 6, 1979 riot in Whitney Hall, a Soledad housing unit, in which one inmate was stabbed to death in his cell and others were wounded. Alexander — who worked as the prison visiting-room photographer and served as the Black representative for B wing on the Men's Advisory Council — was, after an earlier trial ended in a hung jury, convicted of conspiracy to commit murder and conspiracy to commit assault upon an inmate (People v. Alexander, 140 Cal. App. 3d 647, 1983).
profiles.finding: Soledad court case corroborates; Woodyard/Legacy2025 Leonard N Alexander/Yafeu obituary gives long incarceration and is a strong identity/portrait follow-up lead, not yet fully verified.

profiles.name: Patricia Swinton
profiles.description:
Patricia "Pat" Swinton was a New Left radical charged in connection with a wave of bombings of corporate and government buildings in New York City in 1969. Between July and November 1969, eight buildings were bombed by a small group around Sam Melville and Jane Alpert; Melville, Alpert, and David Hughey were arrested in November 1969, but Swinton — who lived under the name "Shoshana" — went underground and remained a fugitive for more than five years.

The FBI captured her on March 12, 1975 at a commune in Vermont. At trial she was acquitted in September 1975. Afterward she said her case illustrated "one of the ways the Government is willing to use its power... to get political dissenters."
profiles.finding: UVA Dengrove archive matches Vermont capture/acquittal but courtroom artwork is not a photo. Milken/TeachPlus teacher portraits rejected as unlinked namesakes.

profiles.name: Carey Junkin
profiles.description: Carey Junkin was a member of the Lexington, Kentucky gay-liberation and lesbian-feminist collective subpoenaed in 1975 by a federal grand jury that was ostensibly hunting the antiwar fugitives Susan Saxe and Katherine Power, but which activists said was being used to map the local radical and gay community. Junkin refused to cooperate and was jailed for civil contempt in March 1975 as one of the six subpoenaed activists who became known as the Lexington Six. He was released on March 31, 1975; of the six, only Jill Raymond held out for the full grand jury term of about fourteen months.
profiles.finding: Lexington Six history, Queer Kentucky review and Contact1975 identify case; no verified individual photograph.

profiles.description: Marla Seymour was a member of the Lexington, Kentucky lesbian-feminist and gay-liberation collective subpoenaed in 1975 by a federal grand jury that was ostensibly hunting the antiwar fugitives Susan Saxe and Katherine Power, but which activists said was being used to map the local radical and gay community. Seymour, then about 22 and openly lesbian, refused to cooperate and was jailed for civil contempt in March 1975 as one of the six subpoenaed activists who became known as the Lexington Six. She spent roughly two months in jail before agreeing to testify and being released; of the six, only Jill Raymond held out for the full grand jury term of about fourteen months.
profiles.finding: Lexington Six sources match; modern school salary/LinkedIn result unverified and rejected for portrait use.
